papers.title: Reliability modeling based on multiple wiener degradation-shock competing failure process and dynamic failure threshold
papers.authors: Anqi Shangguan; Nan Feng; Rong Fei
papers.abstract: <jats:p>Given multiple degradation failure and shock failure processes within the complex system during operation, a reliability model that combines the degradation-shock competing failure process and dynamic failure threshold is modeled. The Wiener process with random effects is considered the degradation process model, which includes random effects to account for the heterogeneity among system units. Then, the extreme shock model with a dynamic failure threshold is used to depict the random shock. The copula function is carried out to illustrate the correlation between multiple degradation processes, the reliability model is constructed further. To verify the application of this model, a numerical case and a micro-electro-mechanical system comprising two micro-mechanical resonators are employed. The parameter sensitivity of the proposed model is analyzed. The study results show that the reliability model, which combines the Wiener process with random effects and the dynamic failure threshold, more accurately reflects the actual operational state of the complex system.</jats:p>

papers.title: Connectivity Maintenance Cost: A Thermodynamic Threshold Model for the Failure Sequence of Sustained Biological Networks, with Application to Neurodegeneration
papers.authors: Sidário Rodrigues Malheiros Júnior
papers.abstract: <jats:p>Living systems are dissipative structures: they persist only while energy flows sustain their internal order. This paper applies that principle at a level not previously formalised — the functional coupling between elements of a biological network. It introduces Connectivity Maintenance Cost (CMC), a threshold model in which coupling between regions of the brain’s connectome requires a minimum continuous energetic expenditure, and in which crossing below this threshold, not element death, is the primary failure event. Network neuroscience explains the connectome’s topology as a trade-off between wiring cost and topological efficiency, but this economic account is a theory of formation with no model of failure; CMC supplies the missing failure term. Five testable propositions are derived from an established thermodynamic and physiological lineage and operationalised using existing imaging modalities. The framework predicts that the clinical sequence of cognitive decline reflects the CMC gradient of the connectome, and that cortical hubs of the default mode network fail first because they carry the highest continuous connectivity cost — a prediction consistent with existing evidence on hub vulnerability to amyloid deposition and with the persistence of clinical decline despite amyloid clearance. Falsification conditions are specified, along with a proposed re-analysis of existing multimodal datasets requiring no new data collection. The framework is positioned relative to wiring-cost economy models of network formation and to the two-hit vascular hypothesis of neurodegeneration, which it extends with a quantitative ordering principle and a candidate mechanism linking hub connectivity to regional vulnerability.​</jats:p>

papers.title: Threshold Effects of Fiscal-Monetary Interdependence and Exchange Rate Regimes in Oil-Dependent Arab Economies
papers.authors: Ibrahim Elbadawi; Mohamed Goaied; Moez Ben Tahar
papers.abstract: This chapter contributes to the literature on fiscal-monetary interdependence in resource-dependent economies in the Arab World, specifically during the post-mid-1990s oil boom. It also provides empirical evidence on threshold effects for oil rents per capita. These findings support differentiated exchange rate regime choices in economies with low rent per capita, such as Sudan and Yemen, relative to wealthier Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) economies and Algeria. The first group suffers from fiscal dominance, which explains their choice of soft pegged exchange rate regimes and their failure to sustain credible exchange rate-based stabilization programs. GCC countries, however, managed to maintain credible de facto pegged exchange rate regimes and convertible currencies, while Algeria graduated to a successfully managed exchange rate regime. Nevertheless, in contrast to Chile and Norway, Arab oil economies still need to establish credible fiscal rules for conducting monetary policy in order to withstand the effects of permanently lower oil prices.

papers.title: Modelling Early Transitions Toward Autonomous Protocells
papers.authors: Ben Shirt‐Ediss
papers.abstract: This thesis broadly concerns the origins of life problem, pursuing a joint approach that combines general philosophical/conceptual reflection on the problem along with more detailed and formal scientific modelling work oriented in the conceptual perspective developed. The central subject matter addressed is the emergence and maintenance of compartmentalised chemistries as precursors of more complex systems with a proper cellular organization. Whereas an evolutionary conception of life dominates prebiotic chemistry research and overflows into the protocells field, this thesis defends that the 'autonomous systems perspective' of living phenomena is a suitable - arguably the most suitable - conceptual framework to serve as a backdrop for protocell research. The autonomy approach allows a careful and thorough reformulation of the origins of cellular life problem as the problem of how integrated autopoietic chemical organisation, present in all full-fledged cells, originated and developed from more simple far-from-equilibrium chemical aggregate systems.
papers.categories: Protocell; Autopoiesis; Living matter; Living systems; Perspective (graphical)

papers.title: A Finite Axiomatic Framework for the Interior Chrysene Lattice and Protocell Organization
papers.authors: Charles D. Schaper
papers.abstract: A finite interior chrysene lattice is defined by molecular cells, ordered attachment ports, compatible directional incidence, an explicit boundary, and specified algebraic and dynamical enrichments. We formulate finite counterparts F1–F12 of the twelve-axiom chrysene framework and prove a recognition theorem: a finite directional graph is an induced lattice region precisely when its edge increments integrate to distinct lattice coordinates and its nearest-neighbor incidence is complete. A 3 × 3 × 3 construction gives a nonempty model with an interior cell and nontrivial plaquettes. Partial translations generate a finite matrix algebra; its tensor extension admits an explicit standard form and a separating spectral seminorm. A distinct edge representation identifies a geometric spectral distance with weighted graph distance. We then define functional realizations, typed partial operations and several inequivalent notions of equivalence. Nonisomorphic path and cycle components realize the same ordered-port control and terminal response, and this response equivalence is preserved under passive interconnection. A fixed AAA carrier supplies reference-invariant external addressing, while a fiber-product construction coordinates genetic, functional and membrane states. A concrete finite-stock model proves compatibility and viability on a specified interval. Theorems about these finite structures require no assertion that geometry alone determines chemistry, chirality, quantum coherence or biological function. Molecular implementations are characterized by an additional common-realization condition.
papers.categories: Mathematics; Lattice (music); Simplex; Finite set; Pure mathematics

papers.title: Adaptation from interactions between metabolism and behaviour:self-sensitive behaviour in protocells
papers.authors: Matthew D. Egbert
papers.abstract: This thesis considers the relationship between adaptive behaviour and metabolism, using theoretical arguments supported by computational models to demonstrate mechanisms of adaptation that are uniquely available to systems based upon the metabolic organisation of self-production. It is argued how, by being sensitive to their metabolic viability, an organism can respond to the quality of its environment with respect to its metabolic well-being. This makes possible simple but powerful ‘self-sensitive’ adaptive behaviours such as “If I am healthy now, keep doing the same as I have been doing – otherwise do something else.” This strategy provides several adaptive benefits, including the ability to respond appropriately to phenomena never previously experienced by the organism nor by any of its ancestors; the ability to integrate different environmental influences to produce an appropriate response; and sensitivity to the organism’s present context and history of experience. Computational models are used to demonstrate these capabilities, as well as the possibility that self-sensitive adaptive behaviour can facilitate the adaptive evolution of populations of self-sensitive organisms through (i) processes similar to the Baldwin effect, (ii) increasing the likelihood of speciation events, and (iii) automatic behavioural adaptation to changes in the organism itself (such as genetic changes). In addition to these theoretical contributions, a computational model of self-sensitive behaviour is presented that recreates chemotaxis patterns observed in bacteria such as Azospirillum brasilense and Campylobacter jejuni. The models also suggest new explanations for previously unexplained asymmetric distributions of bacteria performing aerotaxis. More broadly, the work advocates further research into the relationship between behaviour and the metabolic organisation of self-production, an organisational property shared by all life. It also acts as an example of how abstract models that target theoretical concepts rather than natural phenomena can play a valuable role in the scientific endeavour.

papers.title: Globalization and the erosion of geo-ethnic checkpoints: evolving signal-boundary systems at the edge of chaos
papers.authors: Chris Girard
papers.abstract: Spatial boundaries, thermodynamic–economic specialization, and signal processing are at the core of evolution’s major transitions. Centered on these three dimensions, a proposed evolutionary informatics model roots ethnic and racial cleavages in zero-sum contests over rivalrous resources within geophysical sites. As the geophysical boundaries and signal-processing complexity of social systems coevolved, zero-sum contests centered on metropoles extracting resources from hinterlands. In this colonial extraction process, racialization arose from non-market spatial segregation of populations tagged with hinterland lineage. Subsequent post-industrial erosion—and greater permeability—of racial and ethnic boundaries has been enabled by the progressive uncoupling of more highly evolved complex adaptive systems from geophysical location (non-territorial adaptation). Signal and physical topologies are becoming more distinct. This uncoupling from physical location is driven by cybernetic parallelism in complex adaptive systems: diverse and independent agents learning from their mutual exchange of signals. Cybernetic parallelism has generated epistemic and geopolitical challenges to formal apartheid and racializing immigration policies, but not without friction or reversals.
papers.categories: Complex adaptive system; Ethnic group; Globalization; Geopolitics; Sociology

papers.title: Synthetic cells: Potential benefits and risks of interactions with commensal and pathogenic microorganisms
papers.authors: George B. Stefano
papers.abstract: Synthetic cells are shifting biology from the observation and modification of existing life toward the deliberate construction of cell-like systems. The term, however, includes two biologically different entities: bottom-up protocells assembled from nonliving molecular components and top-down cells whose natural genomes have been minimized, rewritten, or replaced. These two classes occupy the extremes of a much broader landscape of engineered living systems, one that also includes conventional bacteria, yeasts, and mammalian and immune cells carrying synthetic gene circuits, logic programs, and redesigned metabolic pathways. This Perspective is deliberately centered on the two extremes, because they bracket the range of biological autonomy and pose the sharpest contrast between a programmable chemical package and a self-replicating organism; the wider landscape is noted and is drawn upon throughout wherever it bears directly on interaction with microbial communities. Both approaches can clarify the minimum requirements for cellular organization, test hypotheses about the origin and evolution of life, expand biological chemistry, and support programmable sensing or therapy. Their most consequential future setting may not be an isolated laboratory vessel but a microbial ecosystem. Synthetic cells could detect pathogens, intercept virulence signals, deliver antimicrobials locally, support commensal organisms, or restore metabolic functions lost from a disturbed microbiome. The same capacity for molecular communication could also disrupt commensal networks, impose new selective pressures, transfer genetic information, provide exploitable metabolites, or behave unpredictably in complex communities. Because the deep architecture of life—an informational core, a bioenergetic engine, and a membrane-bounded interface under selection—is broadly conserved and governed by conformational matching, engineered constructs will be interpreted through the same molecular languages that natural organisms use to recognize nutrients, competitors, hosts, and threats. It is proposed that synthetic-cell safety should therefore be evaluated relationally: not only by what an engineered cell does alone, but by how natural microorganisms recognize, use, resist, modify, or reorganize around it. Throughout this Perspective, interactions are described as desired or unwanted relative to an explicitly stated design intention, rather than as beneficial or negative, because the same molecular event may be desirable in one ecological and clinical context and unwanted in another. The central challenge is to engineer compatibility where benefit is intended while preserving strong limits on persistence, evolution, and ecological reach.
papers.categories: Protocell; Synthetic biology; Biology; Computational biology; Living systems

papers.title: Membranes as the earliest entropy resisting structures in the origin of life
papers.authors: Yiannis Laouris
papers.abstract: The origin of life remains among the most compelling and debated scientific mysteries. Traditional hypotheses, such as the RNA World and Metabolism-First models, emphasize nucleic acids or metabolic cycles as life’s earliest foundations. However, both approaches inherently assume the existence of structured, stable compartments to maintain molecular interactions; yet do not fully explain their emergence. In this paper, we propose the Membrane-First Hypothesis, asserting that a plausible pathway toward life may have begun with spontaneously forming amphiphilic boundaries that enabled protocellular microenvironments that actively resisted entropy, maintained stable internal environments, and provided primitive localized gradients that bias reaction fluxes. Other prebiotic organizing structures, such as mineral surfaces and coacervate-like droplets, are considered alongside membranes, and their respective advantages and limitations are evaluated. Drawing insights from systems science, including dissipative structures, autopoiesis, hierarchical complexity, and cybernetics, we argue that membranes were not passive containers, but the drivers of differential persistence (‘proto-selection’) and complexity. By systematically comparing existing origin-of-life theories, we propose that membrane-based compartments uniquely integrate metabolic and genetic emergence, offering robust experimental pathways for validation. This systems-science-informed model fundamentally reshapes our understanding of life’s defining origin. We argue that membranes represent one plausible route by which localized, energy-coupled protocellular systems could have emerged prior to fully Darwinian evolution.
papers.categories: Abiogenesis; Protocell; Dissipative system; Darwinism; RNA world hypothesis

papers.title: Quantitative nonequilibrium pathway from fundamental physics to the emergence and persistence of exoplanetary biospheres
papers.authors: Slava G. Turyshev
papers.abstract: We present a physics-based framework that runs from fundamental interactions and constants to biospheres, using a sequence of quantitative nonequilibrium thresholds (“gates”). Each gate is an inequality in measurable variables-free-energy flux, reaction-transport rates, replication fidelity, coding capacity, ecological closure, and climate feedback gains. Crucially, the gate vector is anchored in fundamental physics: dimensionless constants (e.g., the fine-structure constant $$\alpha$$ and mass ratio $${m}_{e}/{m}_{p}$$ ), nuclear resonance placements (e.g., the $${}^{12}\text{C}$$ Hoyle state), and statistical mechanics (Landauer’s bound $${k}_{B}T\ln 2$$ ) fix the energetic, kinetic, and information-theoretic margins that propagate through the gates. This anchoring lets us propagate sensitivities of the constants into biosphere-level metrics (net primary productivity (NPP), cycle-closure ratios, and climate feedback gain), yielding an end-to-end map from constants to biospheres. The framework is predictive: it yields testable inequalities, margin rankings, and population-level correlations between stellar/planetary boundary conditions/biosphere feasibility. It does not claim point-predictions of life prevalence; rather, it specifies which gate margins are observable-bounded versus prior-dominated under explicitly stated chemistry/solvent families and forward models. Darwinian dynamics (heritable variation under selection) appears mid-pipeline; the end of the pipeline is a planet-scale biosphere capable of sustaining positive NPP and closing elemental cycles over geologic time. Questions of prevalence are secondary; our primary objective was to establish a constructive physics → chemistry → biology → genetics → ecosystems pipeline with testable margins and observables. As a result, we recast abiogenesis and biosphere persistence as a gate vector of falsifiable inequalities and map their margins to exoplanet observables, turning the problem into a phase diagram with explicit, testable slack.
papers.categories: Biosphere; Statistical physics; Physics; Non-equilibrium thermodynamics; Dimensionless quantity

papers.title: The evolution of bacterial mechanosensitive channels
papers.authors: Ian R. Booth; Samantha Miller; Axel Müller; Laura E. Lehtovirta‐Morley
papers.abstract: Mechanosensitive channels are ubiquitous and highly studied. However, the evolution of the bacterial channels remains enigmatic. It can be argued that mechanosensitivity might be a feature of all membrane proteins with some becoming progressively less sensitive to membrane tension over the course of evolution. Bacteria and archaea exhibit two main classes of channels, MscS and MscL. Present day channels suggest that the evolution of MscL may be highly constrained, whereas MscS has undergone elaboration via gene fusion (and potentially gene fission) events to generate a diversity of channel structures. Some of these channel variants are constrained to a small number of genera or species. Some are only found in higher organisms. Only exceptionally have these diverse channels been investigated in any detail. In this review we consider both the processes that might have led to the evolved complexity but also some of the methods exploiting the explosion of genome sequences to understand (and/or track) their distribution. The role of MscS-related channels in calcium-mediated cell biology events is considered.
papers.categories: Mechanosensitive channels; Biology; Archaea; Genome; Evolutionary biology

papers.title: High-temperature Gibbs states are uniformly Markovian and trivial
papers.authors: Andrew D. Kim; Tai Hsuan Yang; Jong Yeon Lee
papers.abstract: We prove that, above a constant temperature threshold, Gibbs states of local noncommuting qudit Hamiltonians exhibit exponential decay of mutual information and conditional mutual information (CMI). Specifically, we prove exponential decay of the CMI for arbitrary spatial tripartitions $A \sqcup B \sqcup C$ which need not comprise the entire system, thereby establishing a \textit{uniform Markov property} for high-temperature Gibbs states. A central obstruction to proving such bounds is that conventional cluster expansions for the logarithm of reduced Gibbs states can fail to converge due to noncommutativity. Our main insight is to construct a classical representation of the Gibbs state using an overcomplete basis. Although such representations generally involve negative quasiprobability weights, we show that a decomposition based on projective 2-designs admits a convergent cluster expansion with strictly positive weights at sufficiently high temperatures, allowing us to circumvent the obstruction. The separability of high-temperature Gibbs states is a natural byproduct of this decomposition. Finally, in the context of mixed-state phases of matter, our results imply that high-temperature Gibbs states belong to the same mixed-state phase as the maximally mixed state.

papers.title: Fractional Charge at Dislocations from Band-Inversion Cancellation
papers.authors: Vladimir Juričić; Rodrigo Soto-Garrido
papers.abstract: Band inversions with opposite Chern numbers cancel in the Hall response and yield counterpropagating boundary modes that can gap out. However, a bulk probe of the topology that survives such a cancellation is lacking. We here show that dislocations in inversion-symmetric two-band crystals with cancelling band inversions bind a half-integer charge, which reveals the quantized bulk polarization of the bond-centered obstructed atomic limit realized by such crystals. To demonstrate this, we continuously deform a broad class of two-band lattice models into decoupled chains, without closing the bulk gap or breaking the inversion symmetry, where the dislocation charge follows from a count of occupied bonds. Notably, the fractional part of this charge is insensitive to local perturbations of the dislocation core, and it therefore persists after the in-gap core state is removed, as we show analytically in the chain limit and numerically away from it. In the Weyl-semimetal counterpart, the response to a magnetic flux separates this crystalline charge from the charge set by the Chern number of each momentum slice. We propose that a half-integer core charge that persists after the in-gap peak disappears from the local spectrum can be detected in artificial electronic and optical lattices, with metamaterials providing complementary access to the core modes.

papers.title: AgentRoboCritic: Understanding the Capability of Frontier Agents on Direct Robot Control
papers.authors: Yiyang Du; Yuxuan Kuang; Qitao Zhao; Yixuan Wang; Zhanqiu Guo; Yi Xu; Xin Li; Wenbin He; Liu Ren; Chenyan Xiong
papers.abstract: Frontier multimodal language agents such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated strong capabilities in controlling robots directly via low-level numerical actions without high-level primitives. However, existing benchmarks report only episode-level success rates, which show neither how these agents succeed nor where they fail. In this paper, we present a systematic action-level analysis of frontier agents on direct robot control across 12 manipulation benchmarks. We introduce AgentRoboCritic, an intent-grounded critique framework in which the policy agent states a local intent alongside each action, and a critic evaluates the action's outcome and failure mode against this intent. Our action-level analysis demonstrates the promising capabilities of frontier agents on direct robot control, including closed-loop recovery from local execution failures, reliable semantic grounding across diverse scenes, and strong zero-shot manipulation without task-specific adaptation. It also identifies their current limitations, including task-relevant physical execution bottlenecks such as grasping and alignment, and uneven recovery across failure modes. Finally, we validate our critic on a 400-action human-annotated benchmark and release a dataset of 12,844 annotated actions alongside a fine-tuned open-source critic, Muse-Glimmer-30B, whose failure-mode accuracy rises from 32.58% to 74.24%, enabling low-cost action-level analysis.

papers.title: Depth Pro 2: Sharp and Temporally Consistent Metric Monocular Depth
papers.authors: Peiyun Hu; Marko Mihajlovic; Lyndon Duong; Lahav Lipson; Wei Dong; Amaël Delaunoy; Stephan R. Richter; Vladlen Koltun
papers.abstract: We present Depth Pro 2, an approach to estimating dense metric depth for images and video at full resolution. By analyzing prior methods for monocular depth estimation, we find that they commonly trade off temporal consistency and boundary sharpness: multi-frame methods favor consistency, single-frame methods favor sharpness. To overcome this trade-off, we train a single, scalable network that processes both images and video and predicts depth maps at native resolution. Depth Pro 2 produces depth maps that are metrically accurate, sharp, and temporally consistent all at once, outperforming prior work in all of these dimensions. We release a family of models that define a new Pareto frontier in terms of metric accuracy, sharpness, temporal consistency, and runtime. We release code and weights at https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-depth-pro-2/

papers.title: Local orbital magnetization and Chern markers from equilibrium local currents
papers.authors: Henrique P. Veiga; Aires Ferreira; Caio H. Lewenkopf; João M. Viana Parente Lopes
papers.abstract: Local currents carry the orbital magnetization of a macroscopic sample and are key for modeling inhomogeneous magnetic materials and for understanding magnetoelectric and topological responses. However, producing realistic simulated images of local currents in inhomogeneous systems remains challenging. Building upon recent work on stochastic estimation methods for tight-binding models, we show that all matrix elements of positive semidefinite operators defined on a lattice can be obtained at once from a single set of filtered random vectors. This eliminates the need for independent simulations previously required for off-diagonal elements, which significantly speeds up the calculation of spatial maps of local currents. Further, we express bond currents in terms of loop currents that obey a discrete Poisson equation, with the current vorticity acting as the source term. Its solution yields a local orbital magnetization. In analogy with the global Středa relation, the derivative of this magnetization with respect to the chemical potential defines a new local Chern marker. Built entirely from bond currents, it requires no position operator and is not bound by the zero-sum rule of projector markers in open samples. Hence, it is free of boundary-compensation artifacts, and its sample average converges to the bulk Chern number in a controlled fashion.

papers.title: Realized versus Population Reliability: Anytime-Valid Self-Consistency Certification under Correlated Reasoning
papers.authors: Terence D. Agbeyegbe; Toneukarin G. Agbeyegbe
papers.abstract: Self-consistency certification treats repeated sampling from a language model as sequential evidence accumulation and stops when an anytime-valid e-process crosses a threshold, guaranteeing finite-sample Type I error control by Ville's inequality. Prior constructions assume sampled rollouts are conditionally independent. We show this assumption fails in practice: reasoning streams are positively correlated through shared reasoning prefixes or across-prompt heterogeneity, changing not merely certificate efficiency but the hypothesis certified. Modeling dependence via a per-unit latent state (the random-effects / intraclass-correlation structure) induces exchangeable, equi-correlated increments with correlation $ρ$. Correlation splits the single null into a realized null about the drawn belief and a population null about average model behavior, which coincide only when $ρ=0$. We show: (i) the standard betting e-process remains anytime-valid for the realized null, not the population null; (ii) read as a population-null test, a suitable mixture has asymptotic crossing probability at least $π=P(μ(Z)>0)$, potentially exceeding nominal $ε$; (iii) the within-unit mean's effective sample size saturates at $1/ρ$, so extra within-unit rollouts cannot restore population validity; and (iv) a prompt-level e-process restores population validity, with optimal allocation at one rollout per prompt under a pure rollout budget. Simulations and Claude Haiku 4.5 rollouts confirm this regime dependence: on GSM8K ($\hatρ=0.435$, $\hatθ=+0.96$) the gap is dormant, whereas on AIME ($\hatρ=0.480$, $\hatθ=-0.15$) the single-unit rule crosses on 24% of prompts at nominal $ε=0.05$, while the prompt-level procedure declines (0.00). This correctness result identifies which reliability claim an anytime-valid certificate actually supports under dependence.

papers.title: Global regularity in optimal transportation under the A3w condition
papers.authors: Yuanyuan Li; Xianduo Wang; Xu-jia Wang
papers.abstract: We prove global $C^{2,α}$ and $W^{2,p}$ estimates for potentials in optimal transportation under A3w condition. The cost satisfies condition A3w, and the domains are mutually uniformly $c$-convex with $C^2$ boundaries. We prove global $W^{2,p}$ estimates for positive continuous densities and we obtain global $C^{2,α}$ estimates for positive $C^α$ densities.

papers.title: On Romik's rationality conjectures for critical percolation
papers.authors: Melda Akyazi-Zavadski; Nathanaël Berestycki; Sunil Chhita
papers.abstract:
The completely packed $O(1)$ loop model can be viewed as an interface representation of critical bond percolation on the square lattice. We consider submatching events, which prescribe how these interfaces pair finitely many consecutive boundary points. Romik's rationality conjectures predict that the probabilities of these events on the semi-infinite cylinder are given by specific rational functions, which even become dyadic rationals in the half-plane limit.
  We derive explicit Pfaffian formulae for the probability of $k$ nested arches on the semi-infinite cylinder of circumference $2N$, valid for $k<N$. We deduce that these probabilities are rational functions of $N$ and, by taking the limit $N\to\infty$, that the corresponding half-plane probabilities remain rational. This establishes key aspects of Romik's conjectures.
  Our proof uses identities of Fonseca and Zinn-Justin, derived through the qKZ formalism, which express these probabilities as ratios of enumeration numbers for totally symmetric self-complementary plane partitions (TSSCPPs). These plane partitions admit a dimer representation, allowing us to apply Kasteleyn theory. We evaluate the resulting hypergeometric sum using Zeilberger's and Gosper's algorithms and then take the half-plane limit $N\to\infty$. Along the way, we derive a somewhat simplified expression for the inverse Kasteleyn matrix entries (encoding correlations in TSSCPPs) of Ayyer and Chhita, which might be of independent interest.
